name: Priorat
terms: Denominación de Origen Calificada, a step above DO for regions with a record of consistent quality. Only Rioja and Priorat hold it.
Young wine, sold with little or no aging. Some see a few months in oak.
keyfacts: Priorat is one of only two Spanish regions with DOCa status, alongside Rioja, and is called DOQ in Catalan.
Its soil is llicorella, a brittle, layered slate of darkened copper color, and vine roots push down between its sheets.
Garnatxa negre and Cariñena are the recommended red grapes, and Cabernet Sauvignon, Merlot and Syrah are among the other authorized reds.
Yields are very low, around 1 kg of grapes per vine, against an authorized maximum of 6,000 kg/ha for red grapes.
Vineyards are on steep slopes between about 660 and 2,300 feet, with hot, dry summers and cold winters.

notes: Very old vines on steep schist terraces give tiny yields, around 5 to 6 hectoliters a hectare.
Priorat is dense, rich, concentrated and dark, with noticeable tannin.
It shows dark black fruit with notes of fig and tar.
Reds are Garnacha or Cariñena, alone or blended with grapes such as Cabernet Sauvignon, Merlot or Syrah.

blurb.text: A Catalan DOQ in Tarragona province covering 11 municipalities, one of only two Spanish regions at this top tier, alongside Rioja. It makes powerful reds, which drew international attention in the 1990s, from black slate and quartz soil called llicorella.
